name: Ahiman
title: Anakite Giant in Hebron
summary: Achiman was one of the three sons of Anak, a giant who lived in Hebron. He and his brothers Sheshai and Talmai were seen by the spies that Moses sent into the land of Canaan, and seeing them caused great fear among the Israelites. Achiman and his brothers were later defeated during the conquest of the promised land – according to the book of Joshua they were driven out by Caleb, while the book of Judges attributes the victory to the tribe of Judah. Their defeat illustrates God’s faithfulness in fulfilling the promise of the land, despite seemingly insurmountable obstacles.

keyEvents.title: The Spies See Ahiman in Hebron
keyEvents.description: When Moses sent twelve spies into the land of Canaan, they found Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, descendants of Anak, living in Hebron. The sight of these giants frightened most of the spies.

keyEvents.title: The People's Fear of the Giants
keyEvents.description: The spies' report about the descendants of Anak, including Akiman, caused the people of Israel to be filled with fear and refuse to enter the promised land. The spies said they felt like grasshoppers compared to the giants.

keyEvents.title: Caleb's Promise Regarding Hebron
keyEvents.description: Caleb asked to receive Hebron as his inheritance, even though the descendants of Anak, including Akiman, lived there. He trusted in the Lord's promise and declared himself willing to drive them out.

keyEvents.title: Caleb Drives Akiman Out of Hebron
keyEvents.description: Caleb drove Akiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the three sons of Anak, out of Hebron when he took the city as his inheritance.

keyEvents.title: The Tribe of Judah Defeats the Sons of Anak
keyEvents.description: During the conquest of Canaan, the tribe of Judah attacked Hebron and defeated Sheshai, Akiman, and Talmai, the three sons of Anak.

versions.title: Anakite Giant in Hebron
versions.reason: [minor] Akiman was primarily known as one of the sons/descendants of Anak. The role 'giant' or 'Anakite' would have been more descriptive than simply 'warrior', since his primary function in the biblical text is as a representative of the fearsome Anakites.; [major] In Judges 1:10, Akiman, Sheshai and Talmai are mentioned as having been defeated, but verse 20 concerns Hebron being given to Caleb, who drove out the three sons of Anak. It is more precise to refer only to verse 10 for the actual battle action, and possibly verse 20 separately for the connection with Caleb. Furthermore, the phrasing 'the last giants from the area' is somewhat misleading – the text does not explicitly state that these were the last giants.; [minor] The description says 'thus removed the last giants from the area', but this is an interpretation not directly supported by the text. It would have been more precise to say that they defeated the three sons of Anak.; [minor] The summary states that Akiman was 'driven out' by Caleb, but according to Judges 1:10 he was struck down/killed by the tribe of Judah. It may be useful to mention both traditions (Joshua 15:14 and Judges 1:10) as parallel accounts.; [major] Footnotes are missing. Historical, linguistic and archaeological notes about the Anakites, the name Akiman and the significance of Hebron should be added.

footnotes.text: The name Akiman (Hebrew: אֲחִימַן, Achiman) may mean 'my brother is a gift' or 'brother of a portion,' composed of 'ach' (brother) and 'man' (gift/portion). The name also appears in 1 Chron. 9:17, where it refers to a Levitical gatekeeper—a completely different person.

The Anakim (Hebrew: ענקים, Anakim) were, according to the biblical text, a people of unusually large stature who lived in the hill country around Hebron. They are compared with the Nephilim in Num. 13:33. Some scholars have attempted to link the Anakim to the Egyptian term 'Inw-'nq' found in older Egyptian texts, possibly referring to peoples in southern Canaan.

Hebron (Hebrew: חֶבְרוֹן) is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world. The city was formerly called Kiriath-Arba ('City of Arba'), named after Arba, who according to Josh. 14:15 was the greatest man among the Anakim. Archaeological excavations at Tell er-Rumeide have uncovered settlement traces from the Bronze Age that confirm the city's great age.

There are two parallel accounts of the expulsion of the sons of Anak: In Josh. 15:14 this is attributed to Caleb personally, while in Judg. 1:10 it is the entire tribe of Judah who defeats them. This is a typical example of how the books of Joshua and Judges offer different perspectives on the conquest of Canaan—one more idealized and the other more fragmented.

In Deut. 9:2, Moses refers to the Anakim with the saying: 'Who can stand against the sons of Anak?' This shows that the Anakim's reputation as fearsome warriors was widely known in the ancient world. The fact that Caleb and Judah still overcame them underscores the theme of God's faithfulness to His promise.
